title: What are hidden classes (JEP 371), why were they introduced, how are they created (`defineHiddenClass`), and how do they replace `Unsafe.defineAnonymousClass()`?
shortTitle: Hidden classes (JEP 371) — what they are, why introduced, how created with `defineHiddenClass`, and how they replace `Unsafe.defineAnonymousClass()`

s1_definition.profdef: A hidden class, introduced by JEP 371 in Java 15, is a class that cannot be used directly by the bytecode of other classes — it is not discoverable through normal class loading, has no entry in the class loader's name-to-class table, and can be unloaded independently of its defining class loader. They are created at runtime through the `Lookup.defineHiddenClass` method of `java.lang.invoke.MethodHandles`. They are designed for frameworks that generate classes dynamically, and they officially replace the non-standard, unsupported `sun.misc.Unsafe.defineAnonymousClass()`.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India needs a one-off, custom calculation rule generated on the fly for a single complex trade, and this rule should never appear in the bank's public directory of departments. It is created privately, used by exactly the one service that made it, and quietly disposed of when that service no longer needs it — no other department can look it up by name or call it directly. It is an invisible, private, disposable helper that only its creator knows about. That invisible, creator-only, disposable class is a hidden class.
s1_definition.oneliner: A hidden class is a runtime-generated class that is invisible to normal class loading, usable only through its creator's reference, and independently unloadable — the supported replacement for `Unsafe.defineAnonymousClass`.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A hidden class, introduced by JEP 371 in Java 15, is a class that cannot be used directly by the bytecode of other classes — it is not discoverable through normal class loading, has no entry in the class loader's name-to-class table, and can be unloaded independently of its defining class loader. They are created at runtime through the `Lookup.defineHiddenClass` method of `java.lang.invoke.MethodHandles`. They are designed for frameworks that generate classes dynamically, and they officially replace the non-standard, unsupported `sun.misc.Unsafe.defineAnonymousClass()`.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India needs a one-off, custom calculation rule generated on the fly for a single complex trade, and this rule should never appear in the bank's public directory of departments. It is created privately, used by exactly the one service that made it, and quietly disposed of when that service no longer needs it — no other department can look it up by name or call it directly. It is an invisible, private, disposable helper that only its creator knows about. That invisible, creator-only, disposable class is a hidden class.

**One line to remember:** A hidden class is a runtime-generated class that is invisible to normal class loading, usable only through its creator's reference, and independently unloadable — the supported replacement for `Unsafe.defineAnonymousClass`.

sections.s2_technical:
A hidden class is defined from a byte array of class bytes at runtime, but unlike a normal class it is **not registered** in the class loader's dictionary. That means no other class can refer to it by name in its constant pool, you cannot load it with `Class.forName`, and it does not participate in normal symbolic resolution. The only way to use it is through the `Class` object or `MethodHandles.Lookup` returned when you define it. This makes hidden classes ideal for **framework-generated implementation classes** — lambda bodies, proxies, serializers, expression evaluators — that should be an implementation detail and never part of the public type space.

The reason they were **introduced** is that frameworks had long relied on `sun.misc.Unsafe.defineAnonymousClass()`, an internal, undocumented, unsupported method, to create such throwaway classes efficiently. That method had quirky, poorly specified behaviour, notably an ad-hoc constant-pool patching feature and unclear lifecycle rules, and it was blocking the removal of internal APIs. JEP 371 provided a **standard, supported, well-specified** mechanism so the platform could eventually remove the Unsafe method. The JDK's own lambda metafactory and other machinery moved to hidden classes.

You create a hidden class with **`MethodHandles.Lookup.defineHiddenClass(byte[] bytes, boolean initialize, ClassOption... options)`**. For example: `MethodHandles.Lookup lookup = MethodHandles.lookup(); Class<?> hidden = lookup.defineHiddenClass(classBytes, true).lookupClass();`. The `bytes` are the compiled class file contents. The `initialize` flag says whether to run static initialisers immediately. The `ClassOption` varargs let you request `NESTMATE` (make the hidden class a nestmate of the lookup class, so it shares private access) or `STRONG` (tie its lifetime strongly to the defining loader). The call returns a `Lookup` on the new hidden class, from which you get its `Class` object and can create instances reflectively or via method handles, for example `Object instance = hidden.getConstructor().newInstance();`.

**How it replaces `Unsafe.defineAnonymousClass()`**: the Unsafe method created a VM-anonymous class that was likewise not registered and could be unloaded, but it did so through an unsupported path and bundled a constant-pool patching capability. Hidden classes provide the same core benefits — no name registration, independent unloadability, optional nestmate access — through a public API, while deliberately dropping the unsafe constant-pool patching. Frameworks that generated classes per lambda, per proxy, or per dynamic expression migrate from the Unsafe call to `defineHiddenClass`, gaining a specified lifecycle and better integration with nestmates and modules.

A senior nuance is the **lifecycle and garbage collection** angle, which is why hidden classes save memory: by default a hidden class can be **unloaded** as soon as it is unreachable, even while its defining class loader stays alive, which is important for applications that generate huge numbers of short-lived classes and would otherwise accumulate metaspace. Another nuance is that hidden classes **cannot be the superclass or field type** of normal classes because they are nameless to the resolver, and their names contain an illegal `/` so they can never collide with a real binary name. A final nuance is that hidden classes integrate with **method handles** and `NESTMATE` so generated code can access private members of its host, which is exactly what the lambda metafactory needs.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India has a rules engine that, for certain high-value trades, generates a tiny custom fee-calculation class at runtime from bytecode. This generated class is a pure implementation detail that no other part of the system should be able to look up by name or depend on. We need an invisible, creator-only class. This is exactly a hidden class.

Problem 2 — The bank's old code used the internal `Unsafe.defineAnonymousClass` to do this, which is unsupported and being removed. We need to migrate to the standard `MethodHandles.Lookup.defineHiddenClass` so the code is supported and future-proof. The mini-project shows the modern call.

Problem 3 — The generated fee calculator should be able to be discarded and unloaded once the trade is processed, to avoid metaspace buildup when thousands of trades each generate a class. We show creating the hidden class, instantiating it, invoking it, and letting it become unreachable.

In the mini-project we compile a tiny `FeeRule` implementation to a byte array (shown as reading a pre-compiled class file for clarity), define it as a hidden class with `defineHiddenClass`, instantiate it, invoke its method on a trade amount, and confirm it is not resolvable by name. We log each step and contrast with the deprecated Unsafe approach in comments.

The code contains: a `FeeRule` interface, a `HiddenClassFeeEngine` that defines and uses a hidden class, and a `main`.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile all classes (PercentFeeRule.class becomes the "generated" bytecode payload)
javac -d target/classes src/main/java/com/bank/hidden/HiddenClassDemo.java

# Run (Java 15+ required for defineHiddenClass)
java -cp target/classes com.bank.hidden.HiddenClassDemo

# Verify Java version supports JEP 371
java -version   # must be 15 or higher
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a high-value trade amount of 1,000,000 rupees for which the fee engine will generate and use a hidden fee-rule class.

Step 1 — `main` calls `engine.computeFee(1000000)`. The engine first obtains the bytecode for a class that implements the visible `FeeRule` interface. In production a bytecode generator would emit this; here we read a bundled compiled class as the payload.

Step 2 — The engine obtains a `MethodHandles.Lookup` and calls `defineHiddenClass` with the bytes, `initialize=true`, and the `NESTMATE` option. The JVM creates the class but does not register it in the loader's dictionary. The returned `Class` object is the only handle to it.

Step 3 — The engine logs the hidden class name, which contains a slash and a hash suffix, and confirms `isHidden()` is true. It then tries `Class.forName` on that name and catches `ClassNotFoundException`, proving the class is invisible to normal resolution.

Step 4 — The engine instantiates the hidden class via its no-arg constructor, casts it to the visible `FeeRule` interface, and calls `calculate(1000000)`. The rule computes 0.1% which is 1,000.00 rupees, using `BigDecimal` with half-up rounding to two decimals.

Step 5 — The method returns the fee. Once `hidden` and `rule` go out of scope and become unreachable, the hidden class becomes eligible for independent unloading, freeing metaspace even though the defining loader stays alive.

```
2026-10-26 14:10:15 [INFO] Defined hidden class: com.bank.hidden.PercentFeeRule/0x00000008010a1c40
2026-10-26 14:10:15 [INFO] Is hidden? true
2026-10-26 14:10:15 [INFO] As expected, Class.forName cannot find the hidden class by name
2026-10-26 14:10:15 [INFO] Computed fee for Rs.1000000 trade = Rs.1000.00
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  computeFee(1,000,000)
    │
    ▼
  FeeRuleBytecode.generate() → byte[] (class file for FeeRule impl)
    │
    ▼
  MethodHandles.lookup()
    │ .defineHiddenClass(bytes, true, NESTMATE)
    ▼
  Hidden Class  (name: ...PercentFeeRule/0x....  isHidden=true)
    │ NOT in loader dictionary
    │ Class.forName(name) → ClassNotFoundException
    │ usable only via returned Class reference
    ▼
  hidden.getConstructor().newInstance() → FeeRule instance
    │ rule.calculate(1,000,000) = 1,000,000 × 0.001 = 1000.00
    ▼
  return Rs.1000.00
    │ (hidden + rule unreachable) → hidden class eligible for UNLOAD
```

```
  ┌──────────────────────────┐

  │ HiddenClassFeeEngine                      │

  │   - rule.calculate(amount)                │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Lifecycle: DEFINED → USED → UNREACHABLE → UNLOADED (independent of loader)

  Call Chain:
    1. computeFee(1,000,000)
    2.   bytes = FeeRuleBytecode.generate()
    3.   hidden = lookup.defineHiddenClass(bytes, true, NESTMATE)

    5.   rule = (FeeRule) hidden.newInstance()
    6.   rule.calculate(1,000,000) → 1000.00
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A hidden class, introduced by JEP 371 in Java 15, is a class generated at runtime that is invisible to normal class loading. It has no entry in the class loader's dictionary, so no other class can reference it by name, Class dot forName cannot find it, and it does not take part in symbolic resolution. The only way to use it is through the Class object or method-handles lookup returned when I define it. It can also be unloaded independently of its defining class loader, which is a big deal for frameworks that generate many short-lived classes.

They were introduced to give frameworks a supported replacement for the internal Unsafe dot defineAnonymousClass method. That method was undocumented, unsupported, and had quirky constant-pool patching behaviour, and it was blocking the removal of internal APIs. JEP 371 provides a standard, well-specified mechanism, and the JDK's own lambda machinery moved to hidden classes.

I create a hidden class with MethodHandles dot Lookup dot defineHiddenClass, passing the class bytes, an initialize flag, and class options. The NESTMATE option makes the hidden class a nestmate of my lookup class so it can share private access, and the STRONG option ties its lifetime strongly to the loader. The call returns a lookup on the new class from which I get the Class object and create instances. In my banking project, a fee rules engine generates a tiny fee-calculation class for high-value trades, defines it as a hidden class, instantiates it, and computes the fee, and I can confirm the class is not resolvable by name because Class dot forName throws ClassNotFoundException.

The way it replaces the Unsafe method is that it offers the same core benefits, no name registration, independent unloadability, and optional nestmate access, but through a public, specified API, while deliberately dropping the unsafe constant-pool patching. The payoff in a bank is memory: when thousands of trades each generate a rule class, hidden classes can be unloaded as soon as they are unreachable even though the loader stays alive, so metaspace does not keep growing. That combination of invisibility, controlled access, and independent unloading is exactly what a dynamic rules engine needs.

---

keyPoints: Anonymous class: inline implementation with no name
Used for: one-time event handlers, callbacks, comparators
Can extend a class OR implement one interface (not both)
Captured variables must be effectively final
